tasks.paper_claimed: Martin & Mahoney 2019a/2019b/2021 (avg_alpha, power-law); Bartlett et al. 2020 (stable rank)
tasks.paper_verified: Martin, Mahoney, 'Traditional and Heavy-Tailed Self Regularization in Neural Network Models', arXiv:1901.08276 (2019) and 'Heavy-Tailed Universality Predicts Trends in Test Accuracies', Nature Comms 12:4122 (2021), arXiv:1901.08278 — verified, defines the WeightWatcher power-law exponent alpha fit to the empirical spectral density (ESD) of eigenvalues lambda=sigma^2 of W^T W via the powerlaw MLE package with KS-optimal x_min. Stable rank ||W||_F^2/||W||_2^2 is Bartlett, Foster, Telgarsky, 'Spectrally-normalized margin bounds for neural networks', NeurIPS 2017, arXiv:1706.08498 (cited year '2020' is wrong; should be 2017).
tasks.intuition: The power-law slope of a weight matrix's singular-value spectrum is a training-quality fingerprint: Martin & Mahoney's Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory shows that well-optimized layers develop heavy-tailed spectra (small alpha) reflecting implicit self-regularization and feature specialization, and the layer-averaged exponent tracks generalization across hundreds of pretrained models without any data. Stable rank ||W||_F^2/||W||_2^2 complements this as a soft count of effective directions a weight matrix uses. Both should track LM capability because a model that has learned richly structured, well-conditioned transforms exhibits heavier-tailed, higher-stable-rank weight spectra than an under-trained one.

issues.claim: CITATION: the reported 'alpha' is not Martin & Mahoney's WeightWatcher exponent. The code runs a Hill estimator over a fixed top-20% tail of the SINGULAR VALUES sigma, whereas M&M fit the power-law to the ESD of the EIGENVALUES lambda=sigma^2 of W^T W using the powerlaw-package MLE with a KS-optimal x_min. Because lambda=sigma^2, the code's estimate is approximately 2*alpha_MM - 1, on a different scale.
issues.evidence: spectral.py:59-80 computes `S = torch.linalg.svdvals(W)` then Hill `alpha = 1 + k/sum(log(top_k/x_min))` over `k=0.2*len(S)` singular values (no x_min/KS selection). M&M (arXiv:1901.08278) fit ESD of lambda=sigma^2. Repro: drawing lambda~Pareto(pdf~lambda^-alpha_MM), sigma=sqrt(lambda), the code's Hill-on-sigma gives 3.99/5.05/6.88 for alpha_MM=2.5/3.0/4.0 (i.e. ~2*alpha_MM-1). Production avg_alpha is 5.1-6.1 across the zoo (results/study_v3/aggregated.csv), consistent with the 2x-1 inflation; literature WW alpha is ~2-4.
issues.proposed_fix: Square the singular values before fitting (fit lambda=sigma^2), and replace the fixed-fraction Hill with the powerlaw MLE + KS-optimal x_min (or document the metric as a 'singular-value Hill index', not the M&M alpha). The cross-model monotone transform means ranking is roughly preserved, but reported values are not comparable to published WW alpha.

issues.proposed_fix: Correct the year to 2017.

tasks.comparability_notes: alpha and stable_rank are intensive per-matrix quantities, dimensionless in principle, but: (1) the reported alpha is on the 2*alpha_MM-1 scale (see :1), a uniform monotone transform so ranking is preserved; (2) the fixed 20% tail (vs KS-optimal x_min) means the bias depends on per-matrix spectrum shape, which can vary with matrix aspect ratio across architectures; (3) the huge vocab-shaped lm_head (nn.Linear) is averaged in alongside transformer-block weights, so models with very different vocab/d ratios mix a qualitatively different matrix into avg_alpha/avg_stable_rank. GPT-2 Conv1D inclusion (fix #3) is correctly present (TARGET_MODULES line 36-39).

tasks.paper_verified: arXiv:2509.25359 is 'Geometric Metrics and LLMs: What They Measure and When They Work' (v1 title 'From Internal Representations to Text Quality') by Yusupov, Maksimov, Alaeva, Vasileva, Antipina, Zaitseva, Ermilova, Burnaev, Shvetsov — NO author named Wei. Its finding: 'some metrics (notably Schatten Norm and MOM) mainly reflect output length, and their apparent discriminative power collapses once length is controlled.' Li et al. 2024 MNN (arXiv:2410.10672, Yahan Li/Tingyu Xia/Yi Chang/Yuan Wu) verified: column L2 norms sorted descending, sum top D=min(N,d), after centering + row L2 normalization (reference repo MLGroupJLU/MatrixNuclearNorm confirmed). Garrido et al. RankMe (arXiv:2210.02885, ICML 2023) verified: RankMe(Z)=exp(-sum p_k log p_k), p_k=sigma_k/||sigma||_1+eps on RAW singular values, no centering/row-normalization, attributed to Roy & Vetterli 2007.
tasks.intuition: Schatten-p norms, the nuclear-norm approximation, and RankMe all summarize how the singular-value energy of a layer's token matrix is distributed: a representation that spreads energy across many directions (high effective rank, large nuclear/Schatten-1) is using its capacity richly, while one collapsed onto a few directions concentrates energy in the top singular values. The theory is that more capable models maintain higher-rank, less-collapsed intermediate representations that preserve more linearly-decodable information. These spectral summaries should therefore correlate with capability via the same anisotropy/effective-dimensionality mechanism that motivates matrix entropy and IsoScore.

issues.claim: CITATION: Schatten-p norms are attributed to 'Wei et al. 2025, arXiv:2509.25359' but that paper has no author named Wei (it is Yusupov, Maksimov, Alaeva et al.), and its actual conclusion is the OPPOSITE of the claim in the docstring — it finds Schatten Norm 'mainly reflect[s] output length' and loses discriminative power once length is controlled, rather than 'validating' it as a reference-free text-quality proxy.

Note that row normalization was borrowed from the MNN preprocessing and is not part of the Schatten-norm definition.

tasks.paper_claimed: Wei, Tan, Li, Wang, Huang 2024 — 'Large Language Model Evaluation via Matrix Entropy' (Diff-eRank), arXiv:2401.17139
tasks.paper_verified: Lai Wei, Zhiquan Tan, Chenghai Li, Jindong Wang, Weiran Huang, 'Large Language Model Evaluation via Matrix Entropy' (v1 title; NeurIPS 2024 title 'Diff-eRank'), arXiv:2401.17139 — VERIFIED. Def 4.1: z̄_i=(z_i-z̄)/||z_i-z̄||_2 (center then row-L2), Sigma_S=(1/N)sum z̄_i z̄_i^T with tr(Sigma_S)=1. Eq 2: H=-sum_i lambda_i log lambda_i over eigenvalues. Def 4.3: H(D)=(sum_i H(Sigma_Si))/(n log d) — average per-sentence then divide by log d. Paper uses final-layer hidden states. Reference repo waltonfuture/Matrix-Entropy confirms eig_val = svd(A/trace(A)), eRank=exp(entropy).
tasks.intuition: Matrix entropy is the von Neumann entropy of a layer's centered, row-normalized token covariance: low entropy means the model has compressed its token representations onto a few shared directions (an information bottleneck), high entropy means it spreads them across many. Wei et al. show this falls during training as a model learns to discard redundant information, so a tighter last-layer bottleneck (lower normalized entropy) signals more effective representation learning. Dividing by log d makes the quantity comparable across model widths, and it should track capability because stronger models extract more compact, task-relevant codes from their inputs.

issues.claim: The /log d normalization (paper Def 4.3) over-normalizes in the finite-token regime: with ~128 tokens and d_model up to 8192, the centered covariance has rank <= T-1 << d, so the achievable entropy ceiling is log(T-1)/log(d), which SHRINKS as d grows — injecting a width-dependent downward bias into matrix_entropy_normalized independent of representation quality. This is faithful to the paper (which divides by log d regardless), but is a cross-model comparability caveat.
issues.evidence: matrix_entropy.py:93 `H/math.log(max(d,2))`. Repro on random (128,d): H_normalized = 0.717/0.580/0.537 for d=768/4096/8192, matching the rank-limited ceiling log(127)/log(d) = 0.729/0.582/0.538 — a ~0.18 spread driven purely by d via rank deficiency, not content.
issues.proposed_fix: Document the caveat; optionally normalize by log(min(T-1,d)) or report raw entropy alongside, so width-driven ceiling effects are visible. No change required for paper-faithfulness.

tasks.comparability_notes: Matrix entropy is dimensionless after /log d (matches paper). Residual width bias from rank deficiency when T<d (issue :1). Per-sentence aggregation + last-layer headline match the paper (fix #26 faithful). Uses per_sample=True cache (line 102-107), so no cross-document token mixing (bug #1 avoided). The redundant /trace (line 85) is a harmless no-op since row-normalized rows already give tr=1.
tasks.degeneracy_notes: Robust guards: <2 tokens or d<2 -> nan; <2 rows surviving row-norm -> nan; non-finite/<=0 trace -> nan; lambda clamped to 1e-30 before log (0 log 0 convention). All-non-finite layers -> error dict. float() upcast before svdvals (line 59) handles bf16/fp16. Headline uses max layer key. No determinism issues (no sampling).
tasks.proposed_golden_test: Hand-computable case: Z = [[1,0],[ -1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]] (already centered). Row L2 norms = 1; normalized rows unchanged. Sigma = Z^T Z / 4 = diag(0.5,0.5); eigenvalues (0.5,0.5); H = -2*(0.5 log 0.5) = log 2 = 0.6931; H_normalized = log2/log2 = 1.0 exactly. tasks.paper_verified: Jing, Vincent, LeCun, Tian, 'Understanding Dimensional Collapse in Contrastive Self-supervised Learning', ICLR 2022, arXiv:2110.09348 — VERIFIED. Roy & Vetterli, 'The Effective Rank: A Measure of Effective Dimensionality', EUSIPCO 2007 — VERIFIED: erank=exp(H(p)), p_k=sigma_k/sum|sigma_k| (note: the paper's own definition uses raw sigma, but BLME's utils.effective_rank deliberately uses sigma^2 per fix #35, citing the Gram-matrix/eigenvalue convention). The third reference is unverifiable: no arXiv paper 'The Compression Valley: A Depth-Dependent View of LLM Capability' by Pedrotti/Guo/Jaffe exists; the real compression-valley paper is arXiv:2510.06477 'Attention Sinks and Compression Valleys in LLMs are Two Sides of the Same Coin' by Queipo-de-Llano, Arroyo, Barbero, Dong, Bronstein, LeCun, Shwartz-Ziv.
tasks.intuition: Effective rank measures how many dimensions a layer's hidden-state cloud actually spans; tracking it across depth reveals whether the model preserves a high-dimensional representation or collapses it onto a low-dimensional subspace. Severe collapse (a sharp erank drop) destroys linearly-decodable information and is associated with over-smoothing in deep transformers, so the depth profile of effective rank and its largest single-layer drop are mechanistic proxies for how well a model maintains usable representational capacity. The U-shaped 'compression valley' motif links a mid-network erank dip to the model's information-routing efficiency, which the literature ties to capability.

The genuine compression-valley paper is arXiv:2510.06477 by Queipo-de-Llano et al. (PAPERS.md:73 also misattributes 2510.06477 to 'Pedrotti, Guo').

tasks.intuition: The per-layer profile of weight magnitudes (Frobenius and spectral norm) and stable rank exposes how a model distributes representational work across depth: layers whose norms grow sharply with depth indicate exploding-gradient-prone, poorly conditioned transforms, while uniform, high-stable-rank weights signal well-regularized blocks that use many directions. Because well-trained networks tend toward balanced, well-conditioned layer norms (a corollary of heavy-tailed self-regularization), the uniformity and stable-rank profile should track training quality and hence capability.

tasks.paper_claimed: Rudman, Gillman, Rayne, Eickhoff 2022 — IsoScore: Measuring the Uniformity of Embedding Space Utilization, arXiv:2207.10341 (docstring lines 75, 130; PAPERS.md:75)
tasks.paper_verified: William Rudman, Nate Gillman, Taylor Rayne, Carsten Eickhoff. 'IsoScore: Measuring the Uniformity of Embedding Space Utilization.' Findings of ACL 2022. Correct arXiv id is 2108.07344. (arXiv:2207.10341 is a DIFFERENT paper: 'UFO: Unified Feature Optimization', Xi et al., ECCV 2022.)
tasks.intuition: IsoScore measures how uniformly variance is distributed across all dimensions of the representation space, i.e. how close the empirical covariance spectrum is to a scaled identity (a single scalar in [0,1], 1 = perfectly isotropic). It should track LM capability because anisotropic 'narrow-cone' representations waste embedding capacity, compress semantically distinct tokens into a small subspace, and degrade the linear separability of the residual stream; models that utilize their full dimensional budget can encode more distinguishable features per layer.

issues.claim: CITATION: the cited arXiv id 2207.10341 resolves to an unrelated paper ('UFO: Unified Feature Optimization', ECCV 2022), not IsoScore; the correct IsoScore id is 2108.07344.

issues.claim: The implementation normalizes the eigenvalue vector so its SUM equals d (L1), but the paper's Algorithm 1 normalizes by the L2 norm (Sigma_hat = sqrt(n)*Sigma_D/||Sigma_D||); the resulting scalar is NOT the paper's IsoScore and diverges by up to ~10x on anisotropic spectra.
issues.evidence: isotropy.py:112-118: `s = full.sum(); full = full*(d/s)` (sum-normalisation) then `delta_iso_sq = d*(d-1)`. Paper Algorithm 1 (verified via ar5iv 2108.07344): Step4 'Sigma_hat_D := sqrt(n)*Sigma_D/||Sigma_D||' (L2 norm), Step5 'delta := ||Sigma_hat_D - 1||/sqrt(2(n-sqrt(n)))', Step6 'phi := (n - delta^2(n-sqrt(n)))^2/n^2', Step7 'iota := (n*phi-1)/(n-1)'. Numerical reproduction (CPU, 5000 pts): power-law 1.5^-i, d=64 → code=0.817 vs paper=0.064; d=768 → code=0.804 vs paper=0.005; spectrum (4,2,1,0.5) → code=0.872 vs paper=0.548; isotropic-Gaussian d=768 sample → code=0.9998 vs paper=0.866. On the actual (highly anisotropic) LLM hidden states the code reports near-isotropic (~0.8) where real IsoScore reports ~0.05, inverting the qualitative conclusion and making the published 'isoscore' column wrong relative to the cited metric.
issues.proposed_fix: Replace the sum-normalisation block with the paper's L2 normalisation and delta/phi/iota formulas: sigma_hat = sqrt(d)*lam/np.linalg.norm(lam); delta2 = sum((sigma_hat-1)**2)/(2*(d-sqrt(d))); phi = (d - delta2*(d-sqrt(d)))**2/d**2; iota = (d*phi-1)/(d-1). Validate against the official isoscore package (bcbi-edu/p_eickhoff_isoscore). Re-run affected models.

tasks.paper_verified: Effective rank: Olivier Roy, Martin Vetterli, 'The Effective Rank: A Measure of Effective Dimensionality', EUSIPCO 2007 — p_k = sigma_k/||sigma||_1 (singular values, L1-normalized), erank = exp(-sum p_k ln p_k). tasks.intuition: These SVD diagnostics summarize the singular-value spectrum of the pooled hidden-state cloud: effective rank and participation ratio count how many directions are actively used, condition number and explained-variance AUC measure spectral concentration, and average pairwise cosine measures directional crowding. Higher effective dimensionality indicates the model spreads information across many features rather than collapsing into a dominant subspace, which tends to correlate with richer representations and downstream capability.

A high-rank, semantically clustered, well-aligned unembedding supports sharper next-token discrimination, so these properties plausibly track model quality.

Although LMs are unsupervised, the degree to which topic-coherent inputs cluster tightly and separate cleanly in the final, post-norm representation reflects the linear decodability and abstraction quality of that layer, which plausibly tracks model capability.

Pick v=0.04 → assert NC1 ≈ 0.02 and nc1_subspace_rank == 1.

tasks.paper_claimed: Kornblith, Norouzi, Lee, Hinton 2019 — Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited, ICML 2019, arXiv:1905.00414 (linear CKA, Section 3); Cortes, Mohri, Rostamizadeh 2012 — Algorithms for Learning Kernels Based on Centered Alignment, arXiv:1203.0550
tasks.paper_verified: Simon Kornblith, Mohammad Norouzi, Honglak Lee, Geoffrey Hinton, 'Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited', ICML 2019, arXiv:1905.00414. Defines linear CKA as ||Y^T X||_F^2/(||X^T X||_F ||Y^T Y||_F) with the biased HSIC estimator HSIC(K,L)=tr(KHLH)/(n-1)^2 and the explicit assumption 'these matrices have been preprocessed to center the columns'.
tasks.intuition: Linear CKA measures the degree to which two layers encode the same representational geometry, invariant to orthogonal rotation and isotropic scaling, by comparing the alignment of their token-by-token dot-product similarity structures. Low off-diagonal CKA means successive layers reorganize the representation into distinct computational stages rather than re-expressing the same features, so min/std of off-diagonal CKA index how much non-redundant transformation a network performs across depth. More capable models tend to use their depth to progressively restructure representations, which is the mechanistic reason min_offdiag_cka tracks downstream accuracy.

issues.claim: The task emits a raw integer n_layers as a result key (line 149); because the aggregator's exclude list matches only the bare column 'n_layers', the namespaced feature 'geometry_cka.n_layers' survives into the feature matrix, is LASSO-selected (coef 0.0115), and is a near-perfect architecture/depth proxy (Spearman 0.95 with metadata n_layers).

"n_layers" ...} uses exact-match, not endswith; results/study_v3/analysis/lasso_features.csv contains row `geometry_cka.n_layers,0.01152599...`; verified column present in results/study_v3/aggregated.csv with values {6,12,16,...,64} and Spearman 0.947 vs metadata n_layers. The paper's central claim (§E v2/v3) is that intrinsic geometry predicts capability *beyond* size; a raw depth count leaking into the predictor set undermines that control.

tasks.comparability_notes: Linear CKA is dimensionless and bounded in [0,1], invariant to orthogonal transforms and isotropic scaling, so the CKA scalars themselves are cross-model comparable and need no d_model normalization (consistent with §3.4 leaving ratios untouched). The flat-cloud rows are correctly aligned across layers (cache _sample_lengths order), so per_sample=True is NOT needed here unlike matrix_entropy/schatten. The one comparability defect is the emitted n_layers scalar (issue 1), which is pure architecture metadata.

No NaN/inf propagation observed. fp32 upcast via .float() at line 67 before centering/SVD-free matmuls.

Current test_cka only checks key presence and 0<=avg<=1.

tasks.paper_claimed: Gretton, Bousquet, Smola, Schölkopf 2005 — Measuring Statistical Dependence with Hilbert-Schmidt Norms, ALT 2005; Kornblith et al. 2019 — arXiv:1905.00414 (HSIC→CKA normalization)
tasks.paper_verified: Gretton, Bousquet, Smola, Schölkopf, 'Measuring Statistical Dependence with Hilbert-Schmidt Norms', ALT 2005 (biased empirical HSIC = (1/(n-1)^2) tr(KHLH)); Kornblith et al. 2019 normalizes to CKA(K,L)=HSIC(K,L)/sqrt(HSIC(K,K)HSIC(L,L)). The code's linear-kernel normalized HSIC is exactly this and is mathematically identical to linear CKA, as the docstring states.
tasks.intuition: Normalized linear-kernel HSIC is identical to linear CKA and quantifies statistical dependence between two layers' representations; the task's distinctive output is input-to-layer HSIC, which measures how strongly each layer's activations still depend on the raw embedding. A capable model nonlinearly decorrelates deep representations from surface token identity (low input-to-layer HSIC at depth, high compression), so the rate at which dependence on the input decays across layers reflects how much abstraction the network performs.

Flat-cloud rows are aligned across layers (per_sample not needed). hsic_compression_ratio is a ratio of two normalized quantities so also tokenizer/dimension-independent. The 2000-token cap is uniform across models. No size-leaking scalar is emitted (no n_layers key, unlike CKA).

tasks.paper_claimed: Kriegeskorte, Mur, Bandettini 2008 — Representational Similarity Analysis - Connecting the Branches of Systems Neuroscience, Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience 2; secondary Morcos et al. 2018
tasks.paper_verified: Kriegeskorte, Mur, Bandettini 2008, Front. Syst. Neurosci. 2:4. Verified the paper recommends correlation distance for the RDM ('We suggest using correlation distance (1-correlation) as the dissimilarity measure') and Spearman rank correlation to compare two RDMs ('We therefore use the Spearman rank correlation coefficient to compare them').
tasks.intuition: RSA compares the second-order structure of representations: it builds a representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM) of pairwise distances among inputs at each layer, then correlates RDMs across layers to measure whether layers preserve the same relative similarity geometry even with different feature bases. High adjacent-layer RSA indicates smooth, gradual transformation of the representational manifold; abrupt drops mark layers that reorganize structure. The depth profile of representational continuity reflects how a model distributes its computation and is expected to relate to capability.

issues.claim: rsa_min_continuity_layer is an absolute layer index (argmin over adjacent RSA), which is the exact class of size/depth-proxy column #36 was meant to eliminate; it equals ~n_layers-2 for most models and leaks depth into the analysis (Spearman 0.68 with metadata n_layers, -0.49 with log_n_params), surfacing as a spurious univariate 'predictor' (ρ≈0.66 with benchmarks across 79 rows).
issues.evidence: rsa.py:118 `"rsa_min_continuity_layer": int(np.argmin(adj_arr))`; results/study_v3/aggregated.csv shows e.g. gpt2-small n_layers=12 → 10, gpt2-medium 24 → 22 (i.e. n_layers-2); results/study_v3/analysis/univariate.csv has 79 rows for geometry_rsa.rsa_min_continuity_layer with ρ up to 0.677. #36 de-indexed per-layer *profiles* but this scalar argmin slipped through because it is a single int, not a layer-indexed vector.
issues.proposed_fix: Replace the absolute argmin index with a normalized-depth location z=argmin/(n_layers-1) (per §3.4 z_min convention) or drop it from the feature set; alternatively exclude '*_layer' integer-index scalars in the aggregator.

issues.claim: The RDM uses Euclidean distance (pdist metric='euclidean'), but Kriegeskorte 2008 recommends correlation distance (1-correlation); Euclidean RDMs are dominated by overall activation magnitude, and hidden-state norms grow systematically with depth and differ across model families, biasing cross-layer/cross-model RSA comparisons that the deeper-norm geometry inflates.
issues.evidence: rsa.py:82 `rdm = pdist(X, metric="euclidean")`; paper quote: 'We suggest using correlation distance (1-correlation) as the dissimilarity measure ... normalizes for both the overall activation and the variability of activity across space.' Docstring documents Euclidean (so it is DEVIATES_DOCUMENTED) but deviates from the cited method.
issues.proposed_fix: Use correlation distance (pdist metric='correlation') for the RDM to match Kriegeskorte 2008 and remove the depth-dependent magnitude bias; or document the deviation and demonstrate robustness.

issues.claim: RSA takes the first min(min_tokens,200) rows of the flat (ΣT,D) token cloud (per_sample not used), so the 'conditions' are the first ~1.5 sentences' adjacent tokens — non-representative and highly autocorrelated — rather than a diverse set of stimuli/sentences as in canonical RSA.
issues.evidence: rsa.py:55 `cache.get_hidden_states(layer_idx="all", num_samples=num_samples)` (no per_sample=True); rsa.py:71-80 `n_tokens=min(min_tokens, max_tokens_per_layer=200)`, `X = all_layers[li][:n_tokens]`. With num_samples=20 × ~128 tok the first 200 rows come from the opening 1-2 passages. The comparison is consistent across layers (same tokens) so it is not 'corrupted' in the #1 sense, but the sample is biased to early-corpus content.
issues.proposed_fix: Draw a shared random/even token subset across the whole cloud, or use per_sample mean-pooled sentence vectors as RSA 'conditions' for a more faithful (and less autocorrelated) RDM.

tasks.comparability_notes: Spearman-based RSA outputs are rank correlations (bounded [-1,1], dimensionless) so the rsa_* correlation scalars are cross-model comparable. Two leakage/comparability hazards: rsa_min_continuity_layer is an absolute layer index ≈ n_layers (issue 1), and the Euclidean RDM injects depth/family-dependent magnitude scaling (issue 2). tasks.intuition: Each transformer layer applies a residual update h^{(l+1)} = h^{(l)} + f_l(h^{(l)}); this metric reports the per-token update magnitude relative to the residual-stream norm, ||h^{(l+1)} - h^{(l)}|| / ||h^{(l)}||, averaged and maximized over tokens and layer transitions. Small, uniform ratios correspond to the iterative-refinement regime in which each layer makes incremental, stable adjustments to a shared representation, a regime associated with trainability and smooth feature reuse; spikes mark layers that violently restructure the stream, indicating potential instability or unevenly allocated depth. Because the ratio is dimensionless it is directly comparable across model widths, and its profile summarizes how a model amortizes computation over depth.

tasks.paper_verified: Amari, 'Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning', Neural Computation 10(2):251-276, 1998 — exists, but defines the Fisher information matrix and natural gradient over the PARAMETER space of learning machines ('Information geometry is used for calculating the natural gradients in the parameter space of perceptrons'), not a representation-space gradient-norm metric. No Amari work (including the 2016 Springer book 'Information Geometry and Its Applications') defines mean ||grad_h log P(y|h)||^2 over final hidden states as an LM diagnostic; the docstring's exact title matches at best an obscure 1998 Amari tech report on Bayesian duality theory, also unrelated. Nearest real relatives: Kunstner, Hennig, Balles, 'Limitations of the Empirical Fisher Approximation for Natural Gradient Descent', NeurIPS 2019, arXiv:1905.12558 (empirical Fisher = outer products of data-label gradients; the metric equals tr of this in representation space); Novak et al., 'Sensitivity and Generalization in Neural Networks: an Empirical Study', ICLR 2018, arXiv:1802.08760 (Jacobian-norm sensitivity vs generalization).
tasks.intuition: The metric is the mean squared norm of the gradient of the next-token log-likelihood with respect to the final hidden state, computed in closed form for a linear LM head as grad_h log P(y|h) = W_y - E_p[W]. Because the expectation of grad grad^T over observed labels is the empirical Fisher information of the output distribution in representation space, the reported value is exactly the trace of that empirical Fisher: it quantifies how sharply the model's log-likelihood responds to infinitesimal displacements of the last-layer state. Flat (low) values suggest predictions robust to representation noise, while large values indicate a brittle decision geometry near the unembedding; the hypothesized link to capability transplants sharpness/flatness-generalization intuitions from parameter space into representation space.

tasks.paper_verified: No canonical paper exists, and none is claimed — the registry is honest. Closest relatives: nostalgebraist, 'interpreting GPT: the logit lens' (2020) — decoding hidden states through the unembedding; Geva, Caciularu, Wang, Goldberg, 'Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Vocabulary Space', EMNLP 2022, arXiv:2203.14680. The metric is the cosine (norm-free) version of the correct-token logit, since logit_y = ||h||*||W_y||*cos(h, W_y).
tasks.intuition: Prediction alignment is the cosine similarity between the final (post-norm) hidden state at position t and the unembedding row of the true token at t+1 — i.e., the correct-token logit stripped of both the hidden-state and weight-row magnitudes. It measures how directly the residual stream has rotated to point at the correct output direction by the last layer: since the correct-token logit factorizes as ||h||·||W_y||·cos(h, W_y), this cosine isolates the directional share of the model's predictive confidence from magnitude effects. Models that resolve their prediction cleanly in direction — rather than relying on large but poorly-aimed components — should achieve lower next-token loss at matched norm budgets, which is the mechanistic reason alignment should track capability.

tasks.paper_verified: Kawin Ethayarajh, "How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations? Comparing the Geometry of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 Embeddings", EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, arXiv:1909.00512. Verified via arXiv abstract and full text (ar5iv).
tasks.intuition: Ethayarajh's three measures quantify how much a model re-encodes a word as a function of its context: self-similarity (cosine similarity of the same word across contexts), intra-sentence similarity (homogeneity of token representations within a sentence), and maximum explainable variance (how much of a word's contextual variation a single static direction captures), each baselined against the random-pair anisotropy of the layer. Capable language models are expected to spend upper-layer capacity on context-specific composition rather than recycling static type-level vectors, so low anisotropy-adjusted self-similarity and MEV in deep layers indicate genuine context integration — empirically the property that separates contextual encoders from static embeddings. The per-layer profile of these quantities therefore probes whether depth is being used for contextualization at all.

issues.claim: Intra-sentence similarity is computed as mean pairwise cosine among all tokens in a sentence, but Ethayarajh Definition 2 is the mean cosine between each word vector and the sentence MEAN vector — a numerically different quantity.
issues.evidence: contextualization.py:197-203 calls _cosine_pairwise_mean(h_np) over token pairs. Paper (ar5iv 1909.00512, Def 2): "The intra-sentence similarity of s in layer l is" the average cosine similarity between word representations and their sentence mean vector. For unit vectors mean-cos-to-mean ≈ sqrt(1/n + (n-1)/n · meanpair), so values differ and the mapping depends on sentence length n, which varies by tokenizer.
issues.proposed_fix: Compute s_vec = mean of token vectors per sentence, then average cos(token_i, s_vec) over tokens, per Def 2; keep the pairwise version under a distinct key if desired.

issues.claim: MEV is reported raw only; the paper anisotropy-adjusts all three measures, including MEV, with a dedicated baseline (variance explained by the first PC of uniformly random word representations).
issues.evidence: contextualization.py:190-193,210 emit only raw `mev`; no MEV baseline exists. Paper: "For MEV ... the baseline is the proportion of variance in uniformly randomly sampled word representations that is explained by their first principal component" and "We then subtract from each measure its respective baseline to get the anisotropy-adjusted contextuality measure." The omitted correction is model-dependent: v3 mean_anisotropy_baseline spans 0.17 (llama3.1-70b) to 0.50 (pythia-70m), so raw mean_mev partially measures anisotropy, not static explainability.
issues.proposed_fix: Compute a per-layer MEV baseline as the first-PC variance fraction of ~1000 uniformly sampled token vectors and emit mev_corrected = mev − baseline_mev alongside the raw value.

issues.claim: Special tokens are included: tokenizer() defaults to add_special_tokens=True, so BOS (Llama/Gemma/Qwen) appears in every sample at position 0 with a bit-identical hidden state (causal attention), contributing an exact 1.0 self-similarity entry and an attention-sink vector to the anisotropy baseline and intra-sentence sims, while GPT-2/Pythia (no BOS) are unaffected — a systematic cross-family asymmetry.
issues.evidence: contextualization.py:141-142 `tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=128)` (no add_special_tokens=False); 148 collects all token_ids; 157-159 track every position including position 0. BOS state at position 0 of a causal LM depends only on the BOS embedding, hence identical across all 200 samples → _cosine_pairwise_mean = 1.0 exactly (MEV becomes NaN via the total<=0 guard at line 73-74 and is silently dropped from the mean).
issues.proposed_fix: Tokenize with add_special_tokens=False, or filter token ids in tokenizer.all_special_ids out of token_states, all_states_per_layer, and intra_per_layer.

issues.claim: Memory: every token vector at every layer is retained in fp32 RAM (intra_per_layer keeps full (T,D) arrays per layer per sample) before the ~5 reported layers are selected — ≈ΣT·L·D·4 bytes ≈ 67 GB for an 80-layer/8192-d model at 200×128 tokens, risking OOM/timeout on the v3 70B anchors.
issues.evidence: contextualization.py:126-159 collect for all `per_layer = hidden[1:]` layers; layers_to_report is only computed afterwards at 164-172. For llama3.1-70b: 25,600 tokens × 80 layers × 8192 × 4 B ≈ 67 GB host RAM, plus an extra ~840 MB transient per reported layer at np.asarray (line 179).
issues.proposed_fix: Compute layers_to_report from model config (or after the first sample) and store states only for those layers; optionally fp16 storage for the baseline pool.

tasks.comparability_notes: Cosine-based, so independent of d_model; default 5 evenly spaced layers including first/last gives depth-comparable sampling and the aggregator regroups per_layer.layerN keys into mean/std/slope/quantiles (#36 — confirmed in study_v3/aggregated.csv). Tokenizer dependence is real: words are tracked at token-id level (subwords, punctuation, function words dominate the ≥5-occurrence filter), and n_words_tracked is effectively a tokenizer/vocab statistic (TOP_PREDICTORS.md flags it as tokenizer-linked, partial ρ −0.81). BOS asymmetry (issue 3) splits the zoo by family. Raw mean_mev is not comparable while anisotropy baselines vary 0.17–0.50 across models (issue 2). Known-open Section B item (d) — same-sentence token repeats counted as separate contexts vs the paper's across-context design — remains open and is mitigated, not eliminated, by min_word_occurrences=5 and the baseline subtraction; not re-reported here.
tasks.degeneracy_notes: T<4 samples skipped (line 143); constant/identical word vectors give self-sim 1.0 and MEV NaN (SVD total<=0 guard) which nanmean silently drops; zero-norm vectors guarded via safe_norms; empty layers yield NaN aggregates; no samples → error dict. All sampling RNGs are seeded (default_rng(0)/(1)) — deterministic. No NaN/inf propagation into aggregates beyond documented nanmean skips.

tasks.paper_verified: No canonical paper defines this metric (pooled Spearman of token distance vs attention weight) — it is BLME-custom. Motivation references verified: Ofir Press, Noah A. Smith, Mike Lewis, "Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation", ICLR 2022, arXiv:2108.12409 (ALiBi "biases query-key attention scores with a penalty that is proportional to their distance"); Jianlin Su et al., "RoFormer", arXiv:2104.09864; Shouyuan Chen, Sherman Wong, Liangjian Chen, Yuandong Tian, "Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation", arXiv:2306.15595 (docs misname first author as "Chen, Q.").
tasks.intuition: Healthy autoregressive transformers exhibit a smooth distance-dependent decay of attention imposed by their positional geometry (RoPE rotations, ALiBi-style biases, learned locality): nearer keys systematically receive more mass in positional/local heads. The metric uses the rank correlation between query-key distance and attention weight as a proxy for the structural integrity of that positional geometry; a collapse toward zero would indicate degraded positional encoding and poor context-window utilization, which should track long-context and, more weakly, general LM capability. As implemented, however, the pooled estimator confounds genuine decay with the mechanical 1/row-length shrinkage of softmax rows under the causal mask.

issues.claim: CONFIRMED (known-open Section B item (a)): pooling all (i−j, attention) pairs across causal-mask rows before one Spearman produces a large spurious negative correlation from row normalization alone, and the published values sit near that artifact level.
issues.evidence: positional_decay.py:73-82 pools pairs across rows. Repro simulation (this audit): uniform attention 1/(i+1) per row — zero positional preference — gives pooled Spearman = −0.467 at T=64; with genuine decay+noise, pooled = −0.838 vs per-row mean = −0.583. study_v3/aggregated.csv mean_positional_decay_correlation spans [−0.644, −0.311] (mean −0.475), i.e. the observed cross-model spread straddles the structural −0.47 offset, so a large share of the reported signal is mask geometry, not positional decay.
issues.proposed_fix: Compute Spearman per query row i (distance 1..i vs attention over j<i) for rows with ≥3 entries, then average over rows (optionally length-weighted); emit both per-row mean and the legacy pooled value during one transition release.

The structural pooled-Spearman offset depends on the sequence-length distribution; the eval corpus is pre-truncated to 128 tokens per model tokenizer so T is roughly matched across the zoo, keeping the artifact comparable but compressing real dynamic range (observed v3 spread is only 0.33 wide around the −0.47 artifact). layer_positional_decay.layer_{li} keys are regrouped to mean/std/slope/quantile summaries by the aggregator (#36, confirmed in aggregated.csv). tasks.intuition: Fertility and compression ratio measure how many subword symbols a tokenizer spends per word and per character of text: an efficient tokenizer packs more content into a fixed context window, reduces the number of autoregressive composition steps per fact, and lets model capacity attend to semantics rather than orthographic reassembly. Because newer, better-trained model families also ship larger, better-fitted vocabularies, tokenizer efficiency is simultaneously a genuine contributor to capability and a generation/family confound — which is exactly why BLME tracks fertility, compression, and vocab statistics as explicit confound features (~+0.71 partial ρ, TOP_PREDICTORS §2) rather than as causal capability metrics.

tasks.comparability_notes: By construction comparable across the zoo: identical input texts for every model, fertility denominator (whitespace word count) is model-independent, and the numerator isolates the tokenizer. fertility/compression_ratio/total_tokens are deliberately tokenizer-confound features per TOP_PREDICTORS §2. vocab-dependent outputs (vocab_size, vocab_utilization, normalised_token_entropy) intentionally encode vocabulary scale; at the current 1.7k-token sample, utilization and normalized entropy are nearly deterministic functions of vocab size (issue 2). Identical values within tokenizer-sharing families in v3 (all gpt2 sizes = 1.2157) confirm determinism. Tier 1, no forward pass, no d_model/n_layers dependence.
tasks.degeneracy_notes: Empty dataset → falls back to packaged 20-sentence corpus; total_tokens==0 guarded with error dict; single repeated token gives entropy exactly 0 (p log p with p=1); empty strings contribute 0 tokens/0 words harmlessly; max(1, total_words) guard prevents division by zero; counts chars as Python code points (docstring says UTF-8 chars — equivalent for the English corpus). No RNG, fully deterministic.
tasks.proposed_golden_test: Stub tokenizer that splits every whitespace word into exactly 2 ids drawn from 8 distinct ids: corpus ["aa bb", "cc dd"] → total_words=4, total_tokens=8 → fertility==2.0 exactly; total_chars=10 → compression_ratio==0.8; uniform 8-type distribution → token_entropy==ln(8) and normalised_token_entropy==ln(8)/ln(max(2,vocab_size)).

tasks.paper_claimed: none (docstring has no citation; docs/tasks_geometry.md §18 says "Canonical language modeling metric"; PAPERS.md:118 says "Shannon 1948 (bits-per-character); standard cross-entropy")
tasks.paper_verified: C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication", Bell System Technical Journal 27, 1948 (entropy/cross-entropy in bits); for bits-per-character of English specifically: C. E. Shannon, "Prediction and Entropy of Printed English", Bell System Technical Journal 30:50-64, 1951 (verified: bounds entropy of printed English to 0.6-1.3 bits per letter). Token-level perplexity = exp(mean NLL) is the standard LM evaluation quantity; no further canonical paper needed.
tasks.intuition: Held-out cross-entropy is the language-modeling training objective itself, so corpus perplexity and bits-per-character are the most direct intrinsic measures of LM capability, serving in BLME as Y-variables rather than predictors. BPC divides the model's total code length by a tokenizer-independent unit (characters), making it the cleanest single number for cross-architecture comparison, while the rare/frequent stratification separates fit on the high-frequency head of the token distribution from generalization on the tail, where capability differences between models concentrate.

issues.claim: BPC numerator and denominator use mismatched tokenizations: the NLL comes from cache tokenization (add_special_tokens=True default, truncation at 512) while the chars-side token count re-tokenizes with add_special_tokens=False/truncation=False, so on BOS-adding families BPC is biased low by ~1/T (≈0.8% at T=128) relative to GPT-2-family models, and the two sides diverge for any document longer than 512 tokens outside the study corpus.
issues.evidence: perplexity.py:92 `tokenizer(text, truncation=False, add_special_tokens=False)` and 94-96 count (n_tok−1) tokens; cache.py:351-353 tokenizes with defaults (BOS included) so scored tokens per doc = n_tok (the BOS-conditioned first real token is scored), i.e. numerator covers n_tok tokens but tokens_per_char uses n_tok−1. Study corpus is pre-truncated to 128 tokens so the 512 divergence is latent only.
issues.proposed_fix: Reuse the cached per-sample token counts (cache._sample_lengths − 1, minus special tokens) for total_tokens_for_chars instead of re-tokenizing, or re-tokenize with the same add_special_tokens/truncation settings as the scoring path.

issues.claim: CITATION: docstring lacks any citation; PAPERS.md cites "Shannon 1948" for bits-per-character, but the per-character entropy of English is Shannon 1951 (BSTJ 30:50-64).
issues.evidence: perplexity.py:11-21 (no References section); PAPERS.md:118. Verified: Shannon 1951 "Prediction and Entropy of Printed English" is the BPC source (0.6-1.3 bits/letter bounds); Shannon 1948 defines entropy/bits.
issues.proposed_fix: Add a References block citing Shannon 1948 (cross-entropy) and Shannon 1951 (bits-per-character), and update PAPERS.md:118 accordingly.

issues.claim: Bucket-edge asymmetry on tiny corpora: with n_observed=2 the rare bucket gets max(1,·)=1 id but freq_thresh=max(1, 2−0)=2 leaves freq empty (ppl_freq=+inf while ppl_rare is finite); and within the dominant count-1 tie plateau the rare/freq boundary is decided by token-id lexsort — deterministic but arbitrary inside ties.
issues.evidence: perplexity.py:53-56: rare_thresh=max(1, round(n*0.2)) but freq_thresh subtracts the un-maxed round(n*0.2); line 46 `np.lexsort((observed_ids, observed_counts))` breaks count ties by raw id, which correlates with BPE merge order. Irrelevant at study scale (thousands of observed ids; all 45 present v3 models have finite ppl_rare in [6.6, 225.1], confirming fix #40 works).
issues.proposed_fix: Mirror the max(1,·) guard on the frequent bucket (freq_thresh = min(n−1, n−max(1, round(n*0.2)))) and document the tie-break convention in the docstring.

tasks.comparability_notes: Token-level ppl_overall/mean_nll_nats are tokenizer-dependent (finer tokenizers get lower per-token NLL) — acknowledged by design, with bits_per_char provided as the tokenizer-neutral variant (v3 range 0.566-1.351, plausible). ppl_rare/ppl_freq stratify by each model's OWN tokenizer-specific frequency ranking, so the rare sets are different token populations across models — the metric compares 'each model on its own tail', not a shared tail; worth one sentence in the paper appendix. n_tokens_scored differs per model (tokenizer granularity). gemma4-e4b-it perplexity is nulled in the aggregator per fix #38 (confirmed missing in v3 CSV).
tasks.degeneracy_notes: cnt_total=0 → ppl_overall=inf, mean_nll=NaN, BPC=NaN; n_observed=0 → both buckets empty → ppl_rare/ppl_freq=+inf; n_observed=2 edge gives ppl_freq=+inf (issue 3); BPC wrapped in try/except returning NaN on failure; cache path skips T<2 samples with logits/labels/hidden in lock-step (#31); fully deterministic (lexsort tie-break, no RNG); logits are fp32 on both cache (§C contract) and non-cache (collect_prediction_stats .float()) paths before cross_entropy.

tasks.paper_claimed: none (no docstring; docs/tasks_geometry.md §11: "Derived from general geometric alignment literature [No specific conference paper]"; PAPERS.md:225: "no canonical paper; BLME-custom category coherence")
tasks.paper_verified: No canonical paper exists for the composite task — verdict NO_CANONICAL_PAPER is consistent with PAPERS.md's own assessment. Closest verified antecedents: the relation-consistency and analogy sub-metrics implement the vector-offset / 3CosAdd method of Mikolov, Yih, Zweig, "Linguistic Regularities in Continuous Space Word Representations", NAACL-HLT 2013, pp. 746-751 ("each relationship is characterized by a relation-specific vector offset"; king − man + woman ≈ queen); the hub-skew sub-metric follows Radovanović, Nanopoulos, Ivanović, "Hubs in Space: Popular Nearest Neighbors in High-Dimensional Data", JMLR 11, 2010; kNN purity is standard clustering-evaluation practice.
tasks.intuition: The task asks whether hand-curated semantic categories (months, colors, units, punctuation, ...) form coherent, well-separated clusters in the static token-embedding matrix, and whether relational structure (singular/plural, present/past) is encoded as consistent linear offsets that support analogy arithmetic. The premise, inherited from the word-embedding literature, is that a linearly organized lexical geometry at the input layer reflects a well-trained lexical foundation on which contextual computation builds. Because it probes only the embedding matrix (not contextual states), its link to downstream capability is indirect — closest to a lexical-quality prior — which is consistent with its exclusion from the study's X-variable set.

issues.claim: Cross-model comparability is broken by tokenizer-dependent category membership: only words surviving single-token encoding enter each category, so category composition and size differ across the zoo's 8+ tokenizers, and purity has a model-varying hard ceiling min(|cat|−1, k)/k with fixed k=20 (e.g. seasons has only 14 words → ceiling ≤0.65 before any tokenizer attrition) — while per-category n is never emitted, so nothing downstream can correct for it.
issues.evidence: categories.py:120-129 (single-token filter), 177-196 (purity with fixed k=20, denominator k regardless of category size); assets/categories.json: seasons=14, digits=10, currencies=23 entries. Mitigating context: geometry_categories is absent from BLME_RESEARCH_TASKS and BLME_Y_TASKS (run_study.py:44-94) and from study_v3/aggregated.csv (0 matching columns), so v2/v3 results are not contaminated — but the task ships in the library as a 72-task cross-model diagnostic.
issues.proposed_fix: Emit {cat}_n_tokens for every category and normalize purity by its achievable ceiling (same_cat / min(n_cat−1, k)); longer-term, use a fixed cross-tokenizer word list with mean-of-subword-embedding fallback so membership is constant across models.

issues.claim: Both the no-space and leading-space token variants of a word are added to a category when each is a single token, inflating intra-category coherence with orthographic near-duplicates; relation pairs mix variants across pairs so offset vectors carry a leading-space component, and the analogy search counts the alternate variant of the correct answer as an error.
issues.evidence: categories.py:122-129: `for w in [word, ' ' + word]: ... if tid not in cat_labels: cat_tokens[cat_name].append(tid)` adds BOTH when both encode to one id — verified on GPT-2: "red"→[445] AND " red"→[2266] (both single tokens, both appended). Relation branch (96-111) keeps one variant per word but the choice differs per word: "feet"→39690 (no-space) vs "mice"→only " mice"=10693, so the (foot,feet) and (mouse,mice) difference vectors differ by a space-prefix feature; analogy top-1 (321-327) fails when the nearest neighbor is the other-variant token of the correct word.
issues.proposed_fix: Pick exactly one canonical variant per word (prefer the leading-space form, which is the in-context token for BPE vocabularies; the bare form for SentencePiece), and exclude the unused variant id from the analogy candidate set.

issues.evidence: categories.py:138 and 276 `np.random.seed(42)` followed by np.random.choice; also 360 in _compute_projection. Deterministic for this task, but mutates global state mid-suite.
issues.proposed_fix: Replace with a local rng = np.random.default_rng(42) and rng.choice throughout.

tasks.comparability_notes: Operates purely on the input embedding matrix E = get_embeddings(model) (fp32-cast), so no n_layers/seq-len dependence, but heavy tokenizer dependence: category membership, size, purity ceiling, hub-skew sample size, and the surviving relation pairs all vary with the tokenizer (issues 1-2); for tied-embedding models it doubles as unembedding geometry. d_model enters only through cosine geometry (scale-free). Not run in study v2/v3 (absent from run_study.py task lists and aggregated.csv), so it is library-only — its comparability flaws do not affect published headline numbers but must be fixed or documented before recommending it for cross-model use.
tasks.degeneracy_notes: Per-metric size gates (len(tids)<3/<2/<5 skip); tiny-vocab test mode falls back to full-range replacement candidates; embeddings None → error dict. scipy.stats.skew of constant occurrence counts returns NaN with a catastrophic-cancellation warning (verified) → {cat}_hub_max stays valid but {cat}_hub_skew can be NaN when within-category kNN counts tie exactly. Analogy candidate exclusion zeroes a,b,c but not other in-category duplicates; if d_id coincides with an excluded id (shared word across pairs) the analogy is unwinnable. All randomness seeded (np.random.seed(42)) — deterministic but global-state-mutating (issue 3).
tasks.proposed_golden_test: Stub tokenizer mapping A→0, B→1, C→2, D→3 (single ids, no space variants) over a 6-token vocab with hand-set 2-D embeddings: t0=(1,0), t1=(0.8,0.6), t2=(0.6,0.8) as category 'test', t3=(−1,0), t4=(0,−1), t5=(0.7,−0.7) as background; intra = mean cosine distance over the 3 pairs = 1 − (0.8+0.6+0.96)/3 ≈ 0.2133, inter computable over the fixed random tids; assert test_separation to 1e-6 and test_purity (k=2) == 1.0 exactly.

flagged.claim: CITATION: the reported 'alpha' is not Martin & Mahoney's WeightWatcher exponent. The code runs a Hill estimator over a fixed top-20% tail of the SINGULAR VALUES sigma, whereas M&M fit the power-law to the ESD of the EIGENVALUES lambda=sigma^2 of W^T W using the powerlaw-package MLE with a KS-optimal x_min. Because lambda=sigma^2, the code's estimate is approximately 2*alpha_MM - 1, on a different scale.
flagged.evidence: spectral.py:59-80 computes `S = torch.linalg.svdvals(W)` then Hill `alpha = 1 + k/sum(log(top_k/x_min))` over `k=0.2*len(S)` singular values (no x_min/KS selection). M&M (arXiv:1901.08278) fit ESD of lambda=sigma^2. Repro: drawing lambda~Pareto(pdf~lambda^-alpha_MM), sigma=sqrt(lambda), the code's Hill-on-sigma gives 3.99/5.05/6.88 for alpha_MM=2.5/3.0/4.0 (i.e. ~2*alpha_MM-1). Production avg_alpha is 5.1-6.1 across the zoo (results/study_v3/aggregated.csv), consistent with the 2x-1 inflation; literature WW alpha is ~2-4.
flagged.proposed_fix: Square the singular values before fitting (fit lambda=sigma^2), and replace the fixed-fraction Hill with the powerlaw MLE + KS-optimal x_min (or document the metric as a 'singular-value Hill index', not the M&M alpha). The cross-model monotone transform means ranking is roughly preserved, but reported values are not comparable to published WW alpha.

flagged.claim: The implementation normalizes the eigenvalue vector so its SUM equals d (L1), but the paper's Algorithm 1 normalizes by the L2 norm (Sigma_hat = sqrt(n)*Sigma_D/||Sigma_D||); the resulting scalar is NOT the paper's IsoScore and diverges by up to ~10x on anisotropic spectra.
flagged.evidence: isotropy.py:112-118: `s = full.sum(); full = full*(d/s)` (sum-normalisation) then `delta_iso_sq = d*(d-1)`. Paper Algorithm 1 (verified via ar5iv 2108.07344): Step4 'Sigma_hat_D := sqrt(n)*Sigma_D/||Sigma_D||' (L2 norm), Step5 'delta := ||Sigma_hat_D - 1||/sqrt(2(n-sqrt(n)))', Step6 'phi := (n - delta^2(n-sqrt(n)))^2/n^2', Step7 'iota := (n*phi-1)/(n-1)'. Numerical reproduction (CPU, 5000 pts): power-law 1.5^-i, d=64 → code=0.817 vs paper=0.064; d=768 → code=0.804 vs paper=0.005; spectrum (4,2,1,0.5) → code=0.872 vs paper=0.548; isotropic-Gaussian d=768 sample → code=0.9998 vs paper=0.866. On the actual (highly anisotropic) LLM hidden states the code reports near-isotropic (~0.8) where real IsoScore reports ~0.05, inverting the qualitative conclusion and making the published 'isoscore' column wrong relative to the cited metric.
flagged.proposed_fix: Replace the sum-normalisation block with the paper's L2 normalisation and delta/phi/iota formulas: sigma_hat = sqrt(d)*lam/np.linalg.norm(lam); delta2 = sum((sigma_hat-1)**2)/(2*(d-sqrt(d))); phi = (d - delta2*(d-sqrt(d)))**2/d**2; iota = (d*phi-1)/(d-1). Validate against the official isoscore package (bcbi-edu/p_eickhoff_isoscore). Re-run affected models.

flagged.claim: The paper's only definition of this feature is wrong: the catalogue row describes it as 'Agreement of weight-only vs hidden-state predictions', which corresponds to nothing in the code (actual metric: cosine between the final hidden state and the lm_head row of the true next token) — and prediction_alignment_std is a LASSO-selected feature in the v3 analysis, so the published interpretation of a selected predictor is incorrect.

flagged.claim: The mean cosine carries a model-specific anisotropy baseline (Ethayarajh 2019 showed raw cosines between contextual representations are dominated by a common dominant direction), so cross-model differences partly reflect global anisotropy of h and of the unembedding rows rather than target-specific alignment; no baseline correction is applied.
flagged.evidence: consistency.py:82-89 computes raw cosines only. Expected cos(h, W_rand) differs across models due to anisotropy and concentrates as ~1/sqrt(d_model) only in the isotropic limit; geometry/contextualization elsewhere in BLME applies an anisotropy baseline correction (pack §B item d) but this task does not.
flagged.proposed_fix: Additionally report a baseline-corrected value: prediction_alignment_mean minus the mean cosine between the same hidden states and unembedding rows of random (or frequency-matched) tokens, computed per model; document the raw value's anisotropy dependence.

flagged.claim: Intra-sentence similarity is computed as mean pairwise cosine among all tokens in a sentence, but Ethayarajh Definition 2 is the mean cosine between each word vector and the sentence MEAN vector — a numerically different quantity.
flagged.evidence: contextualization.py:197-203 calls _cosine_pairwise_mean(h_np) over token pairs. Paper (ar5iv 1909.00512, Def 2): "The intra-sentence similarity of s in layer l is" the average cosine similarity between word representations and their sentence mean vector. For unit vectors mean-cos-to-mean ≈ sqrt(1/n + (n-1)/n · meanpair), so values differ and the mapping depends on sentence length n, which varies by tokenizer.
flagged.proposed_fix: Compute s_vec = mean of token vectors per sentence, then average cos(token_i, s_vec) over tokens, per Def 2; keep the pairwise version under a distinct key if desired.

flagged.claim: Special tokens are included: tokenizer() defaults to add_special_tokens=True, so BOS (Llama/Gemma/Qwen) appears in every sample at position 0 with a bit-identical hidden state (causal attention), contributing an exact 1.0 self-similarity entry and an attention-sink vector to the anisotropy baseline and intra-sentence sims, while GPT-2/Pythia (no BOS) are unaffected — a systematic cross-family asymmetry.
flagged.evidence: contextualization.py:141-142 `tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=128)` (no add_special_tokens=False); 148 collects all token_ids; 157-159 track every position including position 0. BOS state at position 0 of a causal LM depends only on the BOS embedding, hence identical across all 200 samples → _cosine_pairwise_mean = 1.0 exactly (MEV becomes NaN via the total<=0 guard at line 73-74 and is silently dropped from the mean).
flagged.proposed_fix: Tokenize with add_special_tokens=False, or filter token ids in tokenizer.all_special_ids out of token_states, all_states_per_layer, and intra_per_layer.

flagged.claim: CONFIRMED (known-open Section B item (a)): pooling all (i−j, attention) pairs across causal-mask rows before one Spearman produces a large spurious negative correlation from row normalization alone, and the published values sit near that artifact level.
flagged.evidence: positional_decay.py:73-82 pools pairs across rows. Repro simulation (this audit): uniform attention 1/(i+1) per row — zero positional preference — gives pooled Spearman = −0.467 at T=64; with genuine decay+noise, pooled = −0.838 vs per-row mean = −0.583. study_v3/aggregated.csv mean_positional_decay_correlation spans [−0.644, −0.311] (mean −0.475), i.e. the observed cross-model spread straddles the structural −0.47 offset, so a large share of the reported signal is mask geometry, not positional decay.
flagged.proposed_fix: Compute Spearman per query row i (distance 1..i vs attention over j<i) for rows with ≥3 entries, then average over rows (optionally length-weighted); emit both per-row mean and the legacy pooled value during one transition release.

flagged.claim: BPC numerator and denominator use mismatched tokenizations: the NLL comes from cache tokenization (add_special_tokens=True default, truncation at 512) while the chars-side token count re-tokenizes with add_special_tokens=False/truncation=False, so on BOS-adding families BPC is biased low by ~1/T (≈0.8% at T=128) relative to GPT-2-family models, and the two sides diverge for any document longer than 512 tokens outside the study corpus.

Study corpus is pre-truncated to 128 tokens so the 512 divergence is latent only.

flagged.claim: Cross-model comparability is broken by tokenizer-dependent category membership: only words surviving single-token encoding enter each category, so category composition and size differ across the zoo's 8+ tokenizers, and purity has a model-varying hard ceiling min(|cat|−1, k)/k with fixed k=20 (e.g. seasons has only 14 words → ceiling ≤0.65 before any tokenizer attrition) — while per-category n is never emitted, so nothing downstream can correct for it.
flagged.evidence: categories.py:120-129 (single-token filter), 177-196 (purity with fixed k=20, denominator k regardless of category size); assets/categories.json: seasons=14, digits=10, currencies=23 entries. Mitigating context: geometry_categories is absent from BLME_RESEARCH_TASKS and BLME_Y_TASKS (run_study.py:44-94) and from study_v3/aggregated.csv (0 matching columns), so v2/v3 results are not contaminated — but the task ships in the library as a 72-task cross-model diagnostic.
flagged.proposed_fix: Emit {cat}_n_tokens for every category and normalize purity by its achievable ceiling (same_cat / min(n_cat−1, k)); longer-term, use a fixed cross-tokenizer word list with mean-of-subword-embedding fallback so membership is constant across models.

flagged.claim: Both the no-space and leading-space token variants of a word are added to a category when each is a single token, inflating intra-category coherence with orthographic near-duplicates; relation pairs mix variants across pairs so offset vectors carry a leading-space component, and the analogy search counts the alternate variant of the correct answer as an error.
flagged.evidence: categories.py:122-129: `for w in [word, ' ' + word]: ... if tid not in cat_labels: cat_tokens[cat_name].append(tid)` adds BOTH when both encode to one id — verified on GPT-2: "red"→[445] AND " red"→[2266] (both single tokens, both appended). Relation branch (96-111) keeps one variant per word but the choice differs per word: "feet"→39690 (no-space) vs "mice"→only " mice"=10693, so the (foot,feet) and (mouse,mice) difference vectors differ by a space-prefix feature; analogy top-1 (321-327) fails when the nearest neighbor is the other-variant token of the correct word.
flagged.proposed_fix: Pick exactly one canonical variant per word (prefer the leading-space form, which is the in-context token for BPE vocabularies; the bare form for SentencePiece), and exclude the unused variant id from the analogy candidate set.
